sn12.21:1.2: The purpose of this discourse (and the next) seems to be to extol dependent origination as a special insight of the Buddha. But it does so artlessly, simply plonking down a series of teachings without connecting them in any way. Editors and translators have tried to smooth it over, but I translate as-is. | The ten powers (of a Realized One) are explained at [mn12:9.1](), where they are followed by the four kinds of self-assurance ([mn12:22.1]()). The powers are found independently at [an10.21]() and [an10.22](), and are claimed by Anuruddha at [sn52.15]()–24. The four kinds of self-assurance are at [an4.8](). | The “divine wheel” (_brahmacakka_) is a synonym for the “wheel of the teaching” (_dhammacakka_). In Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.6, the same term refers to the circle of existence in which all things live.
sn12.21:1.3: This is a recommended meditation ([mn10:38.4]()) leading to perfection ([sn12.23:1.4]()). In one place it exemplifies the Buddha’s teaching, but there it follows organically and is marked as quote ([sn22.78:2.2]()). Here it is simply pasted in after the previous passage. It does not offer an integration between the aggregates and dependent origination; they simply appear side by side.
sn12.21:1.8: This is the abstract principle of dependent origination; see discussion at [sn12.37:2.2](). Again there is no textual link with the previous passages.
